description: Database-backed worker backend for Django's Tasks framework (django.tasks), on Django 5.2 LTS and later. Background tasks run on the database you already have. No broker to provision, secure or back up.
rules: Requires Python 3.12 or later and Django 5.2 or later. Django 6.0 and later ship the Tasks framework in core. On Django 5.2 LTS it comes from the django-tasks backport, so install django-ox[backport] there rather than plain django-ox.
Add django_ox to INSTALLED_APPS and set BACKEND to django_ox.backend.OxBackend in the TASKS setting.
Run python manage.py migrate django_ox before starting a worker.
Start a worker with the ox_worker management command. It is a separate process from the web server, and tasks only execute while a worker is running.
Tasks are ordinary django.tasks tasks. django-ox adds nothing to learn on the producer side, so task functions stay portable across django.tasks backends.

enqueue() is a single INSERT on the default database connection. A task enqueued inside transaction.atomic() becomes visible to workers only when that transaction commits, and disappears on rollback, so transaction.on_commit() is not needed.
Workers claim tasks with SELECT FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED on PostgreSQL and MySQL 8 or later, and with an atomic compare-and-set on databases without SKIP LOCKED, including SQLite.

django_ox.bulk.enqueue_many(task, calls) enqueues one task many times, where calls is a list of (args, kwargs) pairs. It inserts 1,000 rows per INSERT inside one transaction and returns TaskResult objects in input order. Queue, priority and run_after are set once on the task with .using(...).
Execution is at-least-once, so tasks should be written to be idempotent.
Use ox_health to check worker and queue health, and ox_prune to delete finished task rows older than a cutoff.

path("ox/", include("django_ox.urls")) exposes GET /ox/metrics, the queue stats as Prometheus gauges: django_ox_tasks{queue,status}, django_ox_ready_tasks, django_ox_oldest_ready_age_seconds, django_ox_last_claim_age_seconds, django_ox_throughput_per_minute and django_ox_failure_rate. The view has no authentication; wrap it with login_required or restrict it by network. django_ox.metrics.collector() registers the same gauges with an existing prometheus_client registry.
Install with pip install django-ox. Configuration lives in the TASKS setting; the smallest working entry is TASKS = {"default": {"BACKEND": "django_ox.backend.OxBackend"}}.

Backend OPTIONS are MAX_ATTEMPTS (default 3), LOCK_TIMEOUT (300 seconds), BACKOFF_INITIAL (5 seconds), BACKOFF_MAX (600 seconds), TASK_TIMEOUT (None), TASK_TIMEOUTS ({}), TASK_TIMEOUT_GRACE (30 seconds) and SCHEDULES. QUEUES sits beside OPTIONS, not inside it.

TASK_TIMEOUT (seconds, default None) bounds one attempt. At the deadline the worker raises django_ox.exceptions.TaskTimeout inside the task on its own thread, or cancels an async task, and records the attempt as failed and retried on the usual backoff. A thread that has not stopped TASK_TIMEOUT_GRACE seconds later is recorded as failed and the worker exits with code 75 so its supervisor restarts it. TASK_TIMEOUTS maps queue names to their own values; there is no per-task timeout because django.tasks has no field for one. django_ox.deadline() and django_ox.remaining() read the attempt's deadline from inside a task. On a thread a coverage tool or a debugger is watching (a sys.settrace hook, or a sys.monitoring tool with events enabled) nothing is raised inside a sync task: the worker logs timeouts_backstop_only, a task that returns within TASK_TIMEOUT_GRACE is recorded as whatever it did, and one still running then is recorded as failed and recycles the worker. An async task is cancelled at the deadline either way.

An attempt is consumed when a worker claims the task, so a worker dying mid-run counts as an attempt. The retry delay after attempt n is BACKOFF_INITIAL * 2 ** (n - 1), capped at BACKOFF_MAX, with no jitter.

LOCK_TIMEOUT bounds how long a worker may stop refreshing its lease, not how long a task may run. A worker renews the lease every LOCK_TIMEOUT / 3 seconds, so a long task on a live worker is not reclaimed.

Recurring tasks are declared in OPTIONS["SCHEDULES"] with a dotted task path and a five-field cron expression. Every running worker dispatches schedules and a unique constraint makes each tick fire once, so there is no separate scheduler process.
The task function is called outside any transaction. A task that needs select_for_update() or atomic writes opens its own transaction.atomic().

ox_worker --concurrency N is a thread pool inside one process. ox_worker --processes N runs N worker processes under one supervisor, each with its own database connections. A worker process that dies is restarted after one second, doubling to 30 seconds; more than five deaths of one slot in a minute stops the supervisor with exit code 1. For CPU-bound tasks use --processes N --concurrency 1.

django_ox.actions.retry(result_id) requeues a FAILED or LOST task for one more attempt; django_ox.actions.discard(result_id) closes a READY, FAILED or LOST task without running it. A particular running task cannot be interrupted on demand; TASK_TIMEOUT bounds every attempt. Tasks are stored on the default database.

For tests, point TASKS at django.tasks.backends.immediate.ImmediateBackend or django.tasks.backends.dummy.DummyBackend instead of django-ox. On Django 5.2 LTS those paths are django_tasks.backends.immediate.ImmediateBackend and django_tasks.backends.dummy.DummyBackend.
Batches and unique tasks are not in django-ox. They are in Oxpull Pro, a paid add-on; see oxpull.com for its status. django_ox.stats and ox_health are in the free package.
